story:
The biggest baobab in Florida grows in the middle of a traffic circle. When the Florida Forest Service measured it in February 2016, the trunk was 10.57 metres round, the tree 16.8 metres tall and its crown about 24 metres across, enough to make it the state champion of its species.

Young Circle is the roundabout at the centre of downtown Hollywood, and its middle is a city park now, ArtsPark. The City of Hollywood says the park is one of the few places in the United States where you can see five baobabs, an African species it calls the second widest kind of tree in the world. The state register lists two of them. This one stands at the south end. The other, a challenger 8.64 metres round, stands on the west side, about 115 metres away, and the two make one easy stop.

When this tree went in, and who planted it, nobody has written down. Local accounts place it in the 1930s or 1940s. Some writers argue for something far older, reasoning from how slowly baobabs grow in Africa. Neither claim rests on a planting record, so we give no age.

The measurement is from 2016, and the city still names its baobabs as a reason to visit the park. Entry is free. If you have stood under it lately, or know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, more than ten metres round, the widest of the registered pair. It stands at the south end of ArtsPark; the other registered baobab is on the west side, about 115 metres away.

story:
Florida's champion baobab is not the taller of the two the state measured in its own park. Its neighbour on the west side of Young Circle tops it by 30 centimetres, at 17.1 metres, measured four days later in February 2016.

The state register files this one as a Florida Challenger, a tree close enough to the champion on points to be in contention. The difference is in the trunk. This one measured 8.64 metres round, the champion at the south end of the park 10.57, and girth counts most in the register's sum. Its crown spread about 23 metres one way and 20 the other.

Both stand in ArtsPark, the city park that fills the middle of the Young Circle roundabout in downtown Hollywood, about 115 metres apart. The City of Hollywood says five baobabs grow there, which makes the park one of the few places in the United States to see that many together. Only two are on the state register, so the other three are there for anyone who wants to pace them out.

No record says when these trees were planted. Local accounts guess the 1930s or 1940s, and others argue for far older, but nobody has produced a date, so we leave the age empty. The park is free and open from early morning until late evening. If you know the story of how baobabs came to a Hollywood traffic circle, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the taller, narrower of the two registered baobabs, 8.64 metres round. It stands on the west side of ArtsPark at Young Circle, about 115 metres from the champion at the south end.

story:
This mahogany is wider than it is tall. Its crown spreads 38 metres one way and 33 the other over a tree that stands 28 metres high, and it grows next to the restrooms of a suburban park in Plantation.

The Florida Forest Service measured it in June 2024 and lists it as the state champion of its species: 4.17 metres round the trunk, 28 metres tall, and a crown that covers more ground than the tree has height. The register scores a tree on its girth, its height and a quarter of its average crown spread, so here the spread does real work in the sum.

African mahogany is native to West Africa, and this one was planted here, an ocean away from its range. Nobody has published when. The register gives no planting date and neither does the park's own page, so the tree has no age here. A trunk of just over four metres says something about size, not years.

The measurement is recent, which matters in hurricane country. As of June 2024 this one was standing and spreading.

Plantation Woods is a free city park, open from eight in the morning until dusk and closed on Wednesday mornings. No ticket, no tour, only a walk to the restrooms and a look up. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 38 metres across and wider than the tree is tall. It stands next to the restrooms in Plantation Woods Park.

Flamingo Gardens grows Florida's biggest sandbox tree and, about 570 metres away across the same garden, one of the trees chasing it. This is the chaser.

The Florida Forest Service measured it in August 2024 at 3.35 metres round and 26.8 metres tall, with a crown about 22 metres across, and lists it as a Florida Challenger. The champion stands on the west side of the children's garden, 4.04 metres round and above 30 metres high. Two trees of one species on the state register, inside one ticketed garden, says a good deal about the place.

Flamingo Gardens began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and grew into a botanical garden and wildlife sanctuary in Davie, west of Fort Lauderdale. Wikipedia counts 23 Florida champion trees on its grounds, and its list includes a dynamite tree, the other common name of this species. The register places this one in the rainforest ridge area.

Nobody has recorded when it was planted, and nothing ties this trunk to the 1927 homestead, so its age stays blank. Entry to the garden is paid. If you are going for the champion anyway, this one is a short walk on, and makes the pair worth comparing. If you know when it went in, tell us.

The Florida Forest Service lists it as a Florida Challenger, a tree in contention for the state title. It is not tall. At 13.7 metres it is the shortest of the garden's trees on this list, about half the height of the sandbox and candlenut trees nearby, and its crown, roughly 15 metres by 11, spreads less than theirs too. What earns it a place on the register is the trunk.

The garden around it began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and is now a botanical garden and wildlife sanctuary in Davie, west of Fort Lauderdale, with 23 Florida champion trees by Wikipedia's count. story:
Florida's biggest candlenut tree is built like a mast. It rises 24.4 metres on a trunk only 2.29 metres round, and the Florida Forest Service, measuring it in August 2024, ranked it the state champion of its species.

The crown is narrow for that height and uneven, about 13 metres one way and 18 the other. It stands in the tropical rainforest area of Flamingo Gardens in Davie, the stretch of the garden that the narrated tram ride passes through, so you can see it from a seat as well as on foot.

Flamingo Gardens started as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and now holds 23 Florida champion trees, by Wikipedia's count. Three registered trees stand within a short walk in this part of the garden. Besides this candlenut there is a challenger sandbox tree about 120 metres off and a thick-trunked gumbo limbo a little further. The garden's other champions, the earpod and the dynamite tree among them, stand a few hundred metres west.

No one has recorded when this tree was planted, so it has no age on our page. A slim trunk on a tall tree says nothing either way. Entry to the garden is paid. If you know its planting date, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height on a slim trunk, 24.4 metres tall and only 2.29 metres round. It stands in the tropical rainforest area of Flamingo Gardens, which the tram ride passes.

story:
Florida's champion Canary Island date palm grows beside a city parking lot at the foot of a bridge. The Florida Forest Service measured it in February 2016 at 18.9 metres tall, with a trunk 203 centimetres round and a crown about 6.7 metres across, and ranked it the biggest of its species in the state.

It stands just south of the east ramp of the Las Olas Boulevard bridge over the Intracoastal Waterway, on the south side of the sidewalk that runs east of the City of Fort Lauderdale's parking lot. That is the register's own description, and it is more precise than our pin, which is the register's coordinate rather than a fix at the trunk.

The palm wears its growth on the outside. The person who nominated it noted that the old leaf bases on the trunk, the boots, were sloughing off, and judged that the tree had many more years of growth left. The city owns the ground, so there is no gate and no ticket.

Two honest limits. The measurement is ten years old, and the register is the only source we have for this palm, so read the title as the state's verdict of 2016. The common name is for the flowers. Cassia javanica blooms pink and white in late spring, which is when a tree like this earns its place in a garden. Nobody has recorded the dates this particular tree flowers, so take the season from the species rather than from the trunk.

It grows in Flamingo Gardens in Davie, which began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and has become a collection of Florida champion trees. The register gives its location as just "Flamingo Gardens", so our pin is the register's own point, about 110 metres from the garden's challenger sandbox tree, and not a fix on this trunk. story:
By its owner's account, this fig is the largest tree in Florida's entire champion register, of any species. Flamingo Gardens says so on its own botanical garden page, and gives the cluster fig a trunk 649 inches round, about 16.5 metres, a height of 102 feet and a crown 95 feet across.

The state's own record tells it differently. The Florida Forest Service entry, measured in February 2016, has a trunk 14.2 metres round, a height of 27.4 metres and a crown up to about 34 metres wide. The two sets of figures do not match, and we have not found which measurement came later. Either way, the trunk is somewhere between 14 and 16 metres round, the widest the register holds in Broward County.

It is not a native. The garden lists it as a non-native champion, one of 23 Florida champion trees on grounds that began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927. This one stands on the garden's west side, about 37 metres from the earpod tree and 75 from the champion strangler fig, so the three make a single stop. Our pin is the register's point, not a fix on the trunk.

The register measurement is ten years old, and nobody has published when the tree was planted, so it has no age on our page. If you know, tell us. Entry to the garden is paid, and it is open daily from 9:30 am, last entry at 4 pm.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 14 to 16 metres round, wider than any other champion in the garden. It stands on the garden's west side, about 37 metres from the earpod tree.

story:
The species the Buddha is said to have sat beneath grows to state-record size beside a parrot enclosure in Davie. This is Florida's champion bodhi tree, measured by the Florida Forest Service in August 2024 at 26.5 metres tall, with a trunk 5.84 metres round.

Ficus religiosa is the sacred fig of South Asia, the tree Buddhist tradition honours at Bodh Gaya. In Florida it is not wild. Somebody planted this one, and it has grown into a big tree in a garden full of them. Flamingo Gardens began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and now counts 23 Florida champion trees on its grounds.

The register's directions are short. "Near Flamingo Gardens parrot enclosure," it says, and the parrots are the easier landmark to find. Our pin is the register's own point rather than a fix on the trunk. It lands about 34 metres from the garden's pink trumpet tree and a short walk from the champion strangler fig, so several of the garden's record trees can be seen in one loop.

The measurement is two years old, so the title is current. What nobody has written down is when the tree went into the ground, so it has no age on our page. If you know, tell us. Entry to the garden is paid, and it is open daily from 9:30 am to 5 pm, last entry at 4.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 5.84 metres round, on a fig 26.5 metres tall. It stands near the parrot enclosure in Flamingo Gardens, which is how the register itself finds it.

story:
Florida's champion strangler fig spreads its crown 44 metres across, nearly half as wide again as the tree is tall. The Florida Forest Service measured it in October 2024 in the arboretum at Flamingo Gardens: 30.2 metres high, a trunk 8.94 metres round, and that enormous crown, which the register puts at 145 feet at its widest.

Unlike most of the garden's record trees, this one belongs here. Ficus aurea is native to South Florida, a fig that typically begins life as a seed lodged high in another tree and sends its roots down to the ground. Nobody has recorded how this particular one started.

It has company. About 110 metres east, the same register lists a challenger strangler fig, measured the same October day. That one is taller, at 31.4 metres, but its trunk is narrower, and the title stays here. Between and around them stand the garden's cluster fig, which the garden calls the largest tree in the whole state register, and the earpod tree. Flamingo Gardens began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and now counts 23 Florida champions.

Our pin is the register's point in the arboretum, not a fix on the trunk. Nobody has published when the tree took root, so it has no age on our page. If you know, tell us. Entry to the garden is paid, and it opens daily from 9:30 am to 5 pm.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 44 metres across on a tree 30.2 metres tall. It stands in the arboretum at Flamingo Gardens, about 110 metres west of the taller challenger strangler fig.

Planting date not found, no age stated. Alive: lifecheck.py RECENT (iNaturalist observations 2026 within range of the pin, not confirmed to be this individual); flagged for that. Native species. Taller than the champion (103 ft vs 99 ft) but narrower trunk. Pairs with ftl_015, ~110 m west of it; about 69 m east of the published Earpod tree (ftl_001), a different species, so not a twin. Could be told as one stop with ftl_015.
story:
This strangler fig is taller than Florida's champion of its species, and it still is not the champion. The Florida Forest Service measured both trees at Flamingo Gardens on the same October day in 2024. This one reached 31.4 metres, about a metre more than the title holder, on a trunk 8.41 metres round. The champion, about 110 metres west in the arboretum, has the thicker trunk at 8.94 metres and an enormous crown, and the register files this one as a Florida Challenger, the tree next in line.

Ficus aurea is a South Florida native, growing in a garden full of imported giants. The species typically starts as a seed in the branches of another tree and sends roots down to the soil.

The challenger stands close to two of the garden's other record trees. The earpod tree, already on our map, is about 69 metres west by our pins, and the cluster fig, which the garden calls the largest tree in the whole state register, is closer still. Flamingo Gardens began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and counts 23 Florida champions today. Seeing both strangler figs and the cluster fig makes one short walk.

Our pin is the register's point, not a fix on the trunk, and nobody has published when the tree took root. If you know, tell us. Entry to the garden is paid.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the taller of the garden's two registered strangler figs, 31.4 metres high on a trunk 8.41 metres round. It stands about 110 metres east of the champion, near the cluster fig and the earpod tree.
